result:
A small clock ticks on the wall, counting seconds no one is watching.

Somewhere outside, rain is starting to fall on rooftops, turning the streets into glass mirrors. A window opens. A kettle hums. A cat stretches and leaves the warmth of a chair for the sill.

There is a strange freedom in having nothing to say. It feels like standing at a dock before a long voyage, holding a map with no name on it. The water is not dangerous, exactly. It is just unknown. And in that unknownness, anything might happen: a boat might appear, the fog might lift, or the dock might sway into the morning and ask nothing of you but to stand there, breathing.

Sometimes the mind is full of words, but the right one will not come. It waits outside the sentence like a bird on a wire, watching with one bright eye. And then, without warning, it lands.

Maybe that is what writing is. Not building. Not proving. Not trying to become someone wiser or more important than you were this morning. Maybe it is only this: listening to the small sounds of an ordinary life and letting them speak.

The rain keeps falling.
The clock keeps ticking.
The page stays open.

And in the quiet space between one second and the next, something begins.
